deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the opening of a fair-copy section headed 'Die biquadratischen Reste' (Math. 12, fol. 10r). It sets up a counting function that the neighbouring pages use for lattice-point counts. The previous page has a bracket [p,p'] for complex p, p' with rules I–IV, and the multiplication formula [mx] = [x] + [x+1/m] + ... - (m-1)/2. The next page has lattice diagrams over Gaussian integers. All of this points to a lattice-point (Gauss-lemma / Eisenstein-type) approach to biquadratic reciprocity in Z[i].

§1 Definition for real x > 0.
- Count 1 for every integer n with 0 < n < x.
- Count 1/2 for the lower endpoint 0.
- Count a further 1/2 if x itself is an integer.
- The total is denoted [x].
In modern terms: [x] = #{n in Z : 0 < n < x} + 1/2 + (1/2)·1_{x in Z}.

Consequences stated by Gauss:
- If 0 < x < 1 ('ächter Bruch'), there are no interior integers, so [x] = 1/2.
- If x = n is a positive integer, there are n-1 interior integers, so [x] = (n-1) + 1/2 + 1/2 = n = x.
- If m < x < m+1, the interior integers are 1,...,m, so [x] = m + 1/2.

Compact form (mine): [x] = (floor(x) + ceiling(x))/2. Equivalently [x] = x - ((x)), where ((x)) is the Dedekind sawtooth: ((x)) = x - floor(x) - 1/2 for non-integer x, and 0 for integer x. In other words, [x] is the floor function 'symmetrised' by giving boundary points weight 1/2.

§2 Extension to x ≤ 0, 'by analogy'.
- [x] = x when x = 0 or x is a negative integer.
- [x] = -(m + 1/2) when -(m+1) < x < -m.
This agrees with (floor+ceiling)/2 everywhere. It makes [·] odd: [-x] = -[x] for all real x. Check (mine): for m < x < m+1 we have [-x] = -(m+1/2) = -[x]; for integers it is trivial.

§3 Periodicity: for every integer k (positive or negative), [x + k] = [x] + k. This is immediate from the floor/ceiling form, since floor and ceiling both shift by k. It can also be read off directly from §1–2 by cases.

§4 is begun but left empty.

Role: the function weights lattice points on the boundary of a counting region by 1/2. This is exactly what makes the complex bracket [p,p'] of the preceding page additive (rule III) and translation-covariant (rules I, II). It is presumably preparation for counting Gaussian lattice points in triangles and squares, as drawn on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors. Definition, special cases, the extension to negative x, and the identities [-x] = -[x] and [x+k] = [x] + k are all correct.
Minor gap: §1 covers only x > 0, so [0] is first fixed in §2. 'Ächter Bruch' must be read as 0 < x < 1 for the statement [x] = 1/2 to hold.
§3 is asserted without proof. It is valid, including when x and x+k have opposite signs, because the definition coincides with (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2 on all of R.

results.what: Definition of a lattice-count function [x] with half weight for boundary points, [x] = (floor x + ceil x)/2 = x - ((x)), extended as an odd function
results.modern_name: Symmetrised floor / complement of the Dedekind sawtooth function ((x)); mean of floor and ceiling
results.usually_credited_to: Sawtooth ((x)): Dedekind (1892, Dedekind sums), building on Riemann's fragments. The half-weight boundary convention in lattice-point counting is common from Eisenstein/Gauss onward.

results.modern_name: Oddness and integer-translation property of x - ((x))

results.what: Use of this function as a foundation for a lattice-point treatment of biquadratic residues (context with neighbouring pages)
results.modern_name: Lattice-point (Gauss lemma / Eisenstein-style) approach to biquadratic reciprocity in Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844) for published proofs of biquadratic reciprocity. Gauss's Nachlass on biquadratic residues is partly printed in Werke II (Schering) and later volumes.

deep.surprise_reason: The page itself contains only an elementary definition and two trivial identities. What is mildly interesting is Gauss's systematic use of a half-weighted, odd 'sawtooth-complement' counting function inside his biquadratic-residue program, which anticipates Dedekind's ((x)) convention. However, Gauss's lattice-point methods for reciprocity are well known, and fragments of this kind are at least partly published in his Werke, so the novelty is small.

checkable.sympy: f = lambda x: (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2; all(f(Rational(p,q)) == Rational(1,2) for q in range(2,12) for p in range(1,q))
f = lambda x: (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2; all(f(n) == n for n in range(-20,21))
checkable.asserts: [x] = x for every integer x (including 0 and negatives)

checkable.sympy: f = lambda x: (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2; all(f(m+Rational(p,q)) == m+Rational(1,2) for m in range(0,10) for q in range(2,9) for p in range(1,q))
f = lambda x: (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2; all(f(-Rational(p,q)) == -f(Rational(p,q)) for q in range(1,10) for p in range(-30,31))
f = lambda x: (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2; all(f(Rational(p,q)+k) == f(Rational(p,q))+k for q in range(1,8) for p in range(-20,21) for k in range(-6,7))

f = lambda x: (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2; saw = lambda x: 0 if x.is_integer else x - floor(x) - Rational(1,2); all(f(Rational(p,q)) == Rational(p,q) - saw(Rational(p,q)) for q in range(1,10) for p in range(-30,31))

f = lambda x: (floor(x)+ceiling(x))/2; all(sum(f(Rational(p,q)+Rational(j,m)) for j in range(m)) == f(m*Rational(p,q)) + Rational(m-1,2) for m in range(1,8) for q in range(1,8) for p in range(-15,16))
checkable.asserts: Multiplication formula from the previous page: [mx] = sum_{j=0}^{m-1} [x + j/m] - (m-1)/2 (e.g. x=1/3, m=6 gives 9/2 - 5/2 = 2 = [2])

transcription_corrections: Heading: the struck-out folio number reads '430' followed by '/18', i.e. old foliation 430/18 cancelled, new number 10 circled. The transcription is essentially right.
Line 3: the struck word at the start ('liegende') is heavily cancelled and could also be read differently. In any case 'ganze Zahl' alone is the intended text.
The interlinear insertion is 'x' written above 'Grenze', giving 'die letztere Grenze x selbst'. The transcription is correct.
§2: 'auch die Größe x selbst ausdrücken' is correct as read. The page uses '[−x] = −[x]' with an ordinary minus sign.
